The All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi; the Safdarjung

Statement 
Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) under the civil 
registration has got statutory backing under the section 10(2) and 10(3) of the 
Registration of Birth and Deaths Act, 1969. As per the provision, the State 
Governments are required to notify the hospitals/areas under the Act, wherein cause 
of each death occuring in hospitals is to be recorded by medical professionals. 
The scheme has been notified, so far, in 27 States/ UTs. The scheme is mainly 
confined to selected hospitals, generally in urban areas. The proportion of 
registered deaths under the Act is less than 50 per cent. The percentage of medically 
certified deaths to total registered deaths during 1999 was found to be 15.4% as 
compared to 14.9% in the year 1998 whereas the percentage of medically 
certified deaths to urban registered was 41.3% in 1999. The low percentage of 
medically certified deaths is mainly due to non-issuance of notification by some 
of the state governments, non-availability of adequate infrastruture and manpower 
to exercise the control over the receipt of returns from the notified hospitals. 
Since the scheme covers mostly those deaths which occured in the selected medical 
institutions generally located in urban areas, as such, compilation of all India or State 
level estimates on causes of death is not feasible. 
2. In order to fill up the data gaps on causes of death, the Registrar General of India 
has introduced VerbalAutopsy (VA) approach as an integral component of the Sample 
Registration System (SRS), covering all States / UTs both in rural and urban areas 
since 2004. Verbal autopsy is an investigation of chain of events, circumstances, 
symptoms and signs of illness leading to death through an interview of close 
relatives or associates of the deceased. Based on the data on causes of death from 
SRS, periodic reports would be made available on regular basis by pooling the sample 
deaths for three years. Further more, in order to develop bench-mark data on cause 
specific mortality by age and sex, a Special Survey of Death (SSD) has been 
conducted in all States/ UTs by pooling the deaths in Sample Registration System (SRS) 
for the period 2001-03. The fieldwork has already been completed and double 
assignment of cause of death by two independent physicians is in progress. The 
First report on causes of death based on above survey is expected to be brought out 
during 2006 by the Office of Registrar General, India.

Cleft lip in children 
*102. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Mi nister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that around 2.5 million kids in the country suffer 
from cleft lip; 
(b) whether there are no proper medical facilities in the country for 
treatment of this palate defect; 
(c)ifso, whether government propose to set up such facilities to help the 
children to have normal growth; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) No large studies have been carried 
out in India to establish the prevalen ce of cleft lip. However, as per rough 
estimates, the incidence of cleft lip and palate is approximately 1 per  700 to 
1000 children. Considering the population of the country, it is estimated that 
approximately 1.5 million children are having cleft lip and palate. 
36 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
The facilities for management of such deformities require surgical 
interventions and these are available both in public and private hospitals in the 
country. More than 1500 plastic surgeons, pediatric surgeons and maxillofacial 
surgeons are available to operate the cleft lip and palate children in the 
country. Such facilities are available at Central Government Institutions, 
namely Dr. R.M.L. Hospital, New Delh i, Safdarjang Hospital, New Delhi, 
Kalavati Saran Children Hospital, Lady Hardinge Medical College, New Delhi, 
AIIMS, New Delhi, PGIMER, Chandigarh and JIPMER, Pondicherry. 
The Cleft lip and Palate does not lead to any developmental or growth problem in the 
children. 
Revamping of parcel services 
*103. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to revamp its parcel 
services; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the benefits expected as a result thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
(a) to (b) Yes, Sir. Revamping of parcel services is a continuous ongoing process. Parcel 
traffic on Indian Railways is carried either by direct booking at railway parcel offices 
or by leaseholders to whom parcel space in Brakevans (SLRs) or Parcel Vans (VPs) is 
leased out on contract basis for a fixed period. 
To streamline movement of parcel traffic, booking and carriage of parcels has been 
rationalized in February, 2004 and November, 2005. Salient features of the 
rationalization policy are as follows: 
(i)  During transit, unloading and re-loading of parcels at intermediate stations from 
one train to another train is permitted only once within the jurisdiction of the 
originating Zonal Railway. 
 
37

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2006] 
(ii) In additional to above, one change-of-gauge trans-shipment is 
permitted. Trans-shipment of parcels booked from stations on a 
branch line section via the corresponding junction station on the main 
line is also permitted. 
(iii) Loading of parcels from and to intermediate stations served by a 
particular train is also permitted if that train stops for five minutes or 
more. However, relaxation for less than 5 minute stoppage has been 
given for only one station for each train within the jurisdiction of each 
zonal railway. Ordinary passenger trains are exempted from this 
restriction. 
(iv) Booking and carriage of parcel traffic is permitted involving two 
break-of-gauge trans-shipment within Southern Railway jurisdiction. 
(v) Luggage belonging to passengers has been exempted from the purview 
of rationalization scheme. 
Under the parcel leasing policy, some portion of parcel space in passenger 
carrying trains is leased out to the highest bidder through open tenders on 
contract basis for a fixed period. Lease holders aggregate parcels from different 
customers and carry their consignment in leased Brakevans (SLRs) or Parcel 
Vans (VPs). 
Loading and unloading of packages is done by lease holders, Railways are 
assured of full earning capacity of pa rcel space, irrespective of its actual 
utilization, with a view to make the parcel leasing scheme more liberal and 
customer friendly, it is being continuously reviewed from time to time. 
(c) Expected benefits to travelling public, trade and Railways from 
rationalization policy and parcel leasing scheme are as under: 
(i) Overall decongestion of platforms at railway stations. 
(ii) Reduce inconvenience to travelling passengers and ensure their safe 
and free movement at platforms. 
(iii) Improve punctuality of trains. 
(iv) Minimize over carriage of parcels and reduce claim cases. 
38 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) Reduction in transit time for transportation of parcels. 
(vi) Better services through assured & faster transit. 
(vii) Better utilization of parcel space. 
(viii) Improve profitability of this loss-making segment of Indian Railways.

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS):(a) to (c) The National Rural Health Mission 
(NRHM) envisages having Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) for 
one thousand population in every village in ten high focus States namely

Compensation for crop loss 
* 115.  SHRILALIT SURI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether an estimate has been made about the loss caused to the crops in the 
Northern States due to severe weather conditions in the region during the winter of 
2005-06; 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2006] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the Central assistance proposed for th e affected States to compensate 
the farmers for the loss/damage of their crops? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (3HRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) 
and (b) The very low temperature during late December, 2005 and early 
January, 2006 has been reported to have affected some crops in some areas of 
Northern States. The State-wise details are as under:— 
• Punjab: An area of 50,250 ha. under potato is reported to have been 
affected by frost. 
• Haryana: About 50% area out of 7.0 lakh ha. under mustard and 30% 
area out of 1.47 lakh ha. under gram in the State is reported to have been 
affected by the cold wave and low temperature. 
• Rajasthan: About 15.1% (6.783 lakh tonnes) losses to the estimated 
production of mustard crop is reported. 
• Madhya Pradesh: An area of 7,840 ha. of different pulses and other 
crops has been affected due to cold wave and low temperature. 
(c) Damage to crops due to cold wave and low temperature is not treated as 
natural calamity and does not qualify for compensation under Calamity Relief 
Fund (CRF) and National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF). However, the 
National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS) is under implementation in 23 
States and 2 UTs including Haryana, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh. Under 
the scheme, assistance is provided to insured farmers in case their yield falls 
short of specified threshold levels. The scheme is available for loanee and non 
loanee farmers. Farmers availing of crop loan are covered under NAIS.

loan of the farmers as on 31st March,  2004 in the districts declared as 
calamity-affected by the State Government. Rescheduled loan shall be 
repayable over a period of five years, at current interest rates, including

ineligible for fresh credit as their earlier debts have been categorized as 
sub-standard or doubtful shall be re scheduled as per the guidelines so 
that such farmers become eligible for fresh credit.

loans.

including partial waiver of interest or loan to the small and marginal 
farmers who have been declared as defaulters and have beome 
ineligible for fresh credit. Banks have also been advised to review cases 
where credit has been denied on the sole ground that a loan account 
was settled through compromise or write offs. 
• In some parts of the country, farmers face acute distress because of the 
heavy burden of debt from non-institutional lenders (e.g. private 
moneylenders). Banks have been permitted to advance loans to such 
farmers to enable them to come out of the informal sources and have 
access to credit from the banking system.

agricultural loans up to Rs. 50,000 and for agri-business & agri-clinics loans up

Adulteration of Fertilizers, Insecticides and Chemicals 
586. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAI AH: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received complaints regarding adulteration 
of fertilizers, insecticides and chemicals due to which production is declining 
every year; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the steps taken by Government to prevent this malpractice; 
(d) whether any report has been r eceived regarding adulteration of 
fertilizers from Andhra Pradesh during the last two years; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) to (c) No case of large scale adulteration of 
fertilizers, insecticides & chemicals have been reported to the Ministry. By and 
large good quality of fertilizers & insecticides are being sold in the country. Any 
decline in crop yield cannot be attributed to the non-availability of good quality 
fertilizers and insecticides, but rather  various factors like untimely rains, 
unfavourable weather, non adoption of package of practices and imbalanced 
use of fertilizers play important role in crop productivity. 
Fertilizers (Control) Order, 1985 en sures that fertilizers which meet 
the standards of quality laid down in the Order, are sold to the farmers. 
Similarly, the quality and sale of pesticides and insecticides are regulated under 
the provision of Insecticides Act, 1 968. The State Governments/UTs are the 
enforcement agencies and ar e adequately empowered to take appropriate action 
under the provisions of the Fertilizer (Control) Order, 1985/Essential 
Commodities Act, 1955/lnsecticidesAct, 1968. To ensure that farmers get the 
standard quality of inputs, States have been advised to regularly check the 
quality of fertilizers & insecticides. The samples of fertilizers and insecticides 
are periodically drawn by the notifie d inspectors for analysis. Training 
programmes for insecticides and fertilizer Analysts and Inspectors to upgrade 
their knowledge and functional skills in the analysis and enforcement of various 
provisions of Insecticides Act and Fertilizers (Control) Order, are 
98 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
organized, which are followed by periodical review during Zonal 
Conferences. 
(d) and (e) No report on adulternation of Fertilizers in Andhra Pradesh has 
been reported. However, during last two years i.e. 2003-04 and 2004-05 the 
percentage of non-standard fertilizer samples reported by "State Govt, was 1.1 
and 1.7% respectively.

(b) Sugar Development Fund Rules, 1983 provides that in order to 
help potentially viable sick sugar undertakings, in the private or public 
sector, which have been recommended by the Board of Industrial and 
Financial Reconstruction or in the cooperative sector, which have been 
recommended by the Committee for Rehabilitation, shall be eligible for 
sanction of loan for modernization or rehabilitation of the plant and

Loan for modernization or rehabilitation can be granted up to sixty percent

Development Fund up to ninety percent of the eligible project cost provided the 
sugar undertaking contributes a minimum often percent of the project cost from 
its own rescources as promoters contribution. The loans carry a concessional 
rate of simple interest of two percen t below the "bank rate", which currently 
works out to four percent.

been amended to provide for sanction of loan from sugar Development 
Fund, to sugar factories having an installed capacity of 2500 tonnes 
crushed per day or higher provided the project envisages marketable 
surplus of co-generation power and provided at least ten per cent of the 
project cost is met by the sugar factory from its own resources as part of 
the promoters contribution. 
The Government (Ministry of Non conventional Energy Sources) is 
implementing a programme for promotion of optimum surplus power 
generation from bagasse in the sugar mills. The programme provides for 
central financial assistance in the form of interest subsidy varying from one 
per cent to six percent depending upon boiler configuration.

interaction meets, training programmes etc. Several other fiscal incentives are 
available to the enterpreneurs for setting up co-generation projects, viz.

facilitate the Fora for quicker disposal of cases.

Sugar prices 
605. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that sugar prices were growing up since last 
one year due to shortage of sugar production; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction there to and the steps taken or 
proposed to be taken for stabilizing the sugar prices; 
(c) whether Government have exported sugar to other countries, 
particularly Pakistan despite its shortage; and 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) The production of cane sugar in the sugar year 
(October - September) 2004-05 was 130 la kh M.Ts as against the estimated 
production of 182 lakh M.Ts in the current sugar year 2005-06. The average 
retail price of sugar in the four principal markets of the country during the 
calendar year 2004 was in the range of Rs. 13.25 - 19.00 per Kg. whereas in 
the year 2005 it has been in the range of Rs. 17.50-20.50 per Kg. 
(b) To pre-empt unreasonable hike in sugar prices on account unhealthy 
speculative tendency, if any, and creation of artificial shortage by holding 
back the released mandatory free sale sugar quota by unscrupulous sugar 
mills, the Government have, inter-alia, decided to take the following steps 
to stabilize the prices: 
(i) Mandatory sale of free sale quota released for a particular month within 
the stipulated period, 
120 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) Convert the unsold/unders patched quantity of free sale sugar into 
levy sugar, 
(iii) Activate the enforcement/checks of the sugar mills on random basis, 
(iv) Assess the possibility of facilitating imports through Tariff Rate Quota 
mechanism of sugar in long term, notwithstanding the extant operational 
scheme of raw sugar imports under Advance License Scheme. 
(v) Resort to adequate additional release of free sale quota into the open 
market to tame prices. 
(vi) Closely and constantly monitor the price of sugar in the country for

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) and (b) In order to rationalise the allocation of 
foodgrains under the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS), ensure that the 
food subsidy remains targeted towards poor households, and, keeping in view 
the reduced availability of foodgrains in the Central Pool, the Government took 
the following decisions on 6.1.2006: 
(i) For Above Poverty Line (APL) households, allocation of foodgrains to 
State Governments to be fixed on the basis of 20 kg. per family per 
month for the earlier allocation of 35 kg. per family per month, or the 
offtake during 2004-05, whichever is lower. 
(ii) For Below Poverty Line (BPL) and Antyodaya households, the 
allocation of foodgrains to States to be fixed on the basis of 30 kg. per 
family per month from the existing 35 kg. per family per month. 
(iii) The APL Central Issue Prices (C PS) of foodgrains, which were last 
fixed in July, 2001, to be revised upwards by Rs. 85 per quintal and Rs. 95 
per quintal for wheat and rice respectively. 
(iv) The BPL CIPs, which were last fixed in July, 2000 to be continued at the 
same level. 
(v) The Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY ) CIPs at Rs. 2 per kg. and Rs. 3 
per kg. for wheat and rice respectively to be continued without change. 
The main reasons, inter alia, for the above decision were as follows: 
(i) Reduced availability of foodgrains stock in the Central Pool; 
(ii) Increased offtake of foodgrains under the TPDS and welfare schemes; 
(iii) Non-revision of CIPs since 2000-01 despite increase in MSPs; 
(iv) To reduce diversion of foodgrains; 
(v) Since the target group of benefici aries of almost all welfare schemes 
are similar to that of the TPDS; 
(vi) Recommendation of the Parliamentary Standing Committee to exclude 
APL population from the purview of the TPDS.

Grain Bank Scheme in the adivasi areas 
609. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Grain Bank Scheme is being implemented in 
some of the adivasi areas in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and to what extent this scheme has proved to be 
useful for the adivasis; 
(c) whether Government would implement the Grain Bank Scheme in all the 
adivasi areas keeping in view of its success; and 
(d) if so, by when? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. The Village Grain Bank Scheme was 
launched in 199S-97 by Ministry of Tribal Affairs for establishment of Grain 
Banks in tribal areas. Against the sanctioned 4,858 Banks, 1483 Grain Banks 
were set up in adivasi areas of 11 States upto the year 2004. The scheme has 
been transferred to Department of Food and Public Distribution for its revision 
and implementation. The revised scheme has been approved by the Government 
and circulated to the State Government s for implementing in the chronically 
food scarce areas including the adivasi areas. 
The Scheme provides safeguard agai nst starvation during the period of 
natural calamity or during the lean season when the marginalised food insecured 
households do not have sufficient resources to purchase rations. The scheme 
envisages establishment of grain banks by Gram Panchayats through Gram 
Sabhas, Self Help Groups or Non-Govemmental Organisations (NGOs) in 
food scarce village/areas as notified by State Government/UT Administration. 
The Central Government will allocate foodgrains to each Grain Bank @ one 
quintal per family for an average 40 Below Poverty Line (BPL)/Antyodaya 
Anna Yojana (AAY) families which will be released as one time grant on 'free 
of cost basis'. The provision for storage, transportation training and monitoring 
has also been made. The people belonging to BPL/AAY families are eligible 
to become members of the Grain Bank, who will manage the affairs of the 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2006] 
Bank through an executive committee elected by themselves and having at least 
one woman member. 
The Government proposes to implement the revised scheme during the 
remaining period of Tenth Five Year Plan. During 2005-06 and 2006-07 it is 
proposed to establish approximately 12,000 Grain Banks in the country in the 
food scarce areas including adivasi areas.

(c) A well-knit system to monitor distribution of foodgrains and other goods 
being distributed under PDS is already in place. Under the System the 
responsibility for distribution of foodgrains and other goods through PDS 
outlets in a transparent and efficient manner, lies with the respective State 
Governments. However, the following measures have been taken by the 
Government to reach the PDS items to the beneficiaries; 
(i) The Public Distribution System (Control) Order, 2001 was issued in 
order to streamline the functioning of the PDS and to make the same 
more effective and accountable. Any offence committed in violation of 
the provisions of the Order invokes criminal liability under Section 7 
of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. 
(ii) The State Governments and the Union Territory Administrations have 
been asked to actively involve the Panchayati Raj Institutions to monitor 
the functioning of the Fair Price Shops, as a measure of social audit.

Vigilance Committees at the State, District, Block and FPS levels to 
oversee the functioning of PDS.

consumers in a transparent manner, a model Citizen's Charter has been 
issued by the Central Government for adoption by the State 
Governments/UT Administration.

Government visits their allocated States/UTs to conduct review of the 
TPDS. The observations made by the Area Officers in their reports are 
sent to the concerned State Government/UT for taking necessary action.

Thiruvananathapuram, Kolkat a and Guwahati, the State 
Governments/UTs were requested to take immediate necessary steps to 
curb diversion, through inspections, computerisation and effective 
implementation of PDS Control order.

Statement-ll 
FAO/AFMA/INDIA REGIONAL WORKSHOP ON USE OF 
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY IN FOOD AND AGRICULTURAL 
MARKETING IN ASIA, 26-30 SEPTEMBER, 2005, ASHOK HOTEL, 
NEW DELHI, INDIA 
The FAO/AFMA/lndia Regional Workshop on Use of Information 
Technology in Food and Agricultural Marketing in Asia was convened at 
Ashoka Hotel Diplomatic Enclave, 50—B Chankyapuri, New Delhi-110021. 
India from 26th to 30th Sept. 2005. 
Twenty-seven participants representing twelve member agencies from nine 
countries attended. The Workshop discus sed four technical papers and nine 
country reports. It also made a field visit to Mathura and Agra to observe the 
ITC (Private Sector) Initiatives in India on Information Technology (IT) 
application in its agricultural marketing system. 
The Workshop arrived at the following conclusions and 
recommendations: 
1. In the liberalized market era, the major role of Public Sector food and 
agricultural marketing system is to  provide a framework of enhancing 
development as a service provider and not of the controller/regulator. Traders 
in private sector should have a greater development role by providing 
professional management of markets. 
2. IT has, among others, a major role in enhancing education among farmers 
in the following area: 
(i) Standardization and Grading of food and agricultural commodities to 
facilitate e-trading/commerce; 
(ii) Movement and flow pattern of food and agricultural commodities to 
enable decision making with regard to marketing at macro/micro level; 
(iii) Certification system/specifications for domestic and well as export 
markets including imports; 
(iv) Food Quality and safety issues for domestic and overseas markets for 
various food and agricultural commodities; and 
138 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) Organic cultivation/production, documentation and traceability of 
agricultural produce especially for overseas buy years to promote 
exports. 
3. IT should be used in storing information required by farmers, traders, 
exporters, processors and transporters to facilitate retrieval by any body R&D 
institutions should put their findings on electronic media to facilitate easy 
accessibility by market participants. 
4. The AFMA member agen cies involved in food and agricultural 
commodities should have their own websites and on-line resource 
information with facility for generation of electronic reports. 
 
5. Extensive use of IT should be encouraged to educate farmers in Good 
Agricultural Practices or Good Marketing Practices (GMP) including post 
harvest management especially for fresh (fruit and vegetables) produce. 
6. Electronic market directory/atlas-commodity-wise, marketing 
functions/service-wise weather/rainfall-wise etc. should be make available for 
macro as well as micro-level to facilitate its use by all stake holders of food and 
agricultural commodities. 
7. IT should be popularized in promoting direct marketing between 
producers and buyers i.e. traders, processors exporters, retail agencies, 
consumers including electronic auction system, for transport and efficient 
marketing and better net returns for the agricultural producers, as is being done in 
Korea, Philippines, Malaysia etc. 
8. Farmers require more than 30 kind of information (portfolios to be 
delivered) such as weather, immigration, input availability, input prices, pest and 
disease control, commodity prices/marke ts, crop loans, insurance, licensing, 
registrations, credit, on-line sales/purchases, subsidies, promotional schemes, 
training, farmers markets etc. IT has a major role in providing all such kinds of 
information simultaneously to masses to improve decision making. Similarly 
businessmen and other market participants also require various kinds of reliable 
information, which can be regularly updated and provided through IT. 
9. Electronic Display Boards at village levels with their connectivity to 
markets, weather departments and telephone connectivity are other IT 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2006] 
media to educate and inform the farm ers. Considering the enormous task 
involved, this could be considered under Public Private Partnership to makea it 
finacially self sustainable. 
10. IT has a wide role in Commodity Exchanges, Farmer Advisory 
Services and toll free access to prices/a gricultural queries by farmers from 
time to time. This also covers future price projections/trends, information on 
infrastructure availability at micro level and in the markets. All kinds of static and 
dynamic information related to food and agricultural marketing need to be made 
available through IT. 
11. Content generation to educate farmers to achieve desirable changes in 
knowledge, attitude, skills and behaviour of farmers in very crucial for its 
dissemination through IT. The workshop felt that food and agricultural price, 
which is useful to farmers should be regularly undertaken. This would 
facilitate forecast of prices based on price cycles and other relevant factors. 
12. Grass root level research studies are required on what crops are 
produced? How much of local production is consumed locally? How much goes 
outside? How much of different crops comes from outside for local 
consumption? Such studies would help marketing extensionist to advise on 
product planning. 
13. Micro-level studies on monitoring supply/demand of food and 
agricultural commodities are essential for marketing extensionist to educate 
farmers with regard to where to send? When to send? And in what form to sent 
which often confronts the farmers while taking marketing decisions. 
14. Village level IT kiosks backed with proper marketing extension 
contents under both PPP and private sect or should be encouraged to provide 
wider access to farmers for marketing technology and to achieve desirable 
change in their knowledge, attitude, skills and behaviour. 
15 Multimedia CDs should be prepared on each and every aspect of food 
and agricultural marketing to educate farmers at village level itself. 
16. The organizations dealing with individual or multiple aspects of food 
and agricultural marketing viz. transactional methods, storage, credit, 
standardization and grading, quality and safety of food, transportation, 
140 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
import/export requirements. Sanitary and Phyto-Sanitary (SPS) measures etc. 
should take up educating producers through IT to enable them to enhance 
their income. For this purpose, they should develop their own 
websites/portals, which are freely accessible to farmers through village level IT 
kiosks. The participants however agreed unanimously that unless marketing 
extension enhances farmers net income, it will have no takers. 
17. Many of the existing marketing extension information and 
knowledge, for example, lowest-highest prices, arrivals of produce and markets 
etc. are not readily usable by farmers for decision making. There is a need for a 
mechanism to translate such information in a user-friendly form for the benefit 
of farmers. 
18. Apex R&D institutions in food and agricultural marketing should 
come together to develop farmer friendly contents for dissemination. 
19. Agriculture being the backbone of economy in developing countries, 
infrastructure viz power, internet connectivity, teledensity, cheaper IT 
technologies etc. should be addressed by the Governments on priority for 
upliftment of farmers and rural people.

†620. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per the survey conducted by the Central 
Pollution Control Board, Ganga is the most polluted river in the country; 
(b) if so, the factors responsible for it; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
148 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the condition of other rivers in the country and the places where rivers 
are more polluted, State-wise; and 
(d) the steps taken/being taken by Government to check pollution in these 
rivers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) As per a 
study conducted by the central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), river Ganga 
is designated as moderately polluted river in the country due to enough 
dilution available in most of its stretches for waste assimilation. The river is 
polluted in segments downstream of large townships located along its bank due to 
domestic and industrial discharges. The water quality of the river shows the 
Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD), an indicator of organic pollution and 
bacterial parameters violating the designated-best-use criteria for bathing 
quality in some stretches of the river. The level of Dissolved Oxygen (DO) 
however, remains generally higher than the desired limits throughout its 
length. 
(c) Based on the data of National Water Quality Monitoring Network, the 
CPCB has identified 71 polluted stretches on different rivers in the country. A 
list of polluted river stretches in various states is enclosed as Statement (See 
below). 
(d) The Ministry launched the Ganga Action Plan (GAP) for pollution 
abatement of the river in 1985, the Phase-I of which was completed on 31-3-
2000. Under this programme, works were taken up in 25 Class-I towns in UP, 
Bihar and West Bengal and a sewage treatment capacity of 835 million liters 
per day was created. However, the industrial pollution has been tackled at source 
through the implementation of legal provisions under the Water (Prevention and 
Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. 
The GAP-I was further extended to GAP Phase-ll which covered the main 
tributaries along with the river Ganga. The programme was subsequently 
extended to other Indian rivers in the form of National River Conservation Plan 
(NRCP). In 1996, the GAP Phase-li was merged with NRCP which presently 
covers pollution abatement works in 160 towns spread over 20 states and 34 
rivers in the country.

168 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) 
Environmental degradation is caused by rapid growth of population, 
industrial pollution, unplanned urbanization and unsustainable production and 
consumption patterns. Area under forest and tree cover, quality of water 
resources, air quality etc; are some of the parameters for perceiving level of 
environmental degradation. The State of Forest Report 2003 indicates that the 
forest cover in the country is 678,333 km2 and constitutes 20.64 per cent of its 
geographic area. A comparison with the forest cover assessment of 2001 receals 
an overall increase of 2,795 km2 or 0.41 per cent in forest cover of the country. 
In so far as air quality is concerned, ambient concentrations of respirable 
suspended particulate matter (RSPM), the main pollutant of public health 
concern, appeared to fall between 1993 and 2002 in the metropolitan cities of 
Delhi, Kolkota, Mumbai, Hyderabad and Chennai. The level of sulphur 
dioxide (S0 2) also declined during the same period. However, suspended 
particulate matter (SPM) levels did not fall in proportion to RSPM. 
The water quality monitoring results obtained by the Central Pollution 
Control Board (CPCB) in collaboration with State Pollution Control Boards 
(SPCBs) during the past three year s indicate that organic terms of 
biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and coliform count gives the indication of 
extent of water quality degradation in different parts of our country. It had 
been found that 67% of the observations, out of nearly 3,000 observations are 
having BOD less than 3 mg/l, 18% between 3 to 6 mg/L and 15% above 6 mg/l. 
Similarly, total faecal co liform, which indicate presence of pathogens in 
water are also of major concern. In order to improve the water quality of the 
rivers, the Ministry is implementing the National River Conservation Plan by 
providing assistance to the State Governments. 
(c) and (d) Emission of greenhouse gases resulting from use of fossil fuels is 
the main cause of human interference with the climate system. According to the 
India's Initial National Communication, energy, agriculture and industrial 
processes respectively contribute 61%, 28% and 8% of carbon dioxide 
equivalent (C02 equivalent) emissions. With a shift from

generation through wind, small hydro, biomass and solar energy; socially 
oriented programmes to meet rural energy demand such as the National Project 
on Biogas Development (NPBD) and the Integrated Rural Energy Progamme 
(IREP); solar energy programmes for applications like lighting, water heating, 
cooking and water pumping and research and development covering o cean 
energy, photovoltaic, hydrogen energy, fuel cells, and alternate fuels for

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKALAKSHMI): (a) to (c) Death of poultry had been 
reported from Navapur Taluka of District Nandurbar, Maharashtra, Preliminary 
investigations had indicated the possibility of Newcastle (Raniket) disease but confirmed 
as Avion Influenza H5NI by High Security Animal Disease Laboratory (HSADL), 
Bhopal. 
A series of strategic actions have been initiated immediately on confirmation of 
Avian Influenza. The contingency plans have been put into operation. These action 
include declaration of infected (3 Kms.) and surveillance areas (upto 10 Kms), absolute 
ban on movement of poultry or its products in infected areas, closure of poultry and egg 
markets and shops, destruction of affected poultry followed by proper disposal and 
vaccination of birds in the surveillance are etc. Containment operation will extend to 
cover some poultry in adjoining areas in Uchchhal Tehsil of Surat district in Gujarat 
State also. 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India deputed its Rapid 
Response teams to Maharashtra on 16th February and to Gujarat on 19th February, 2006. 
The teams are in the field and assisting the State Health authorities in carrying out 
active surveillance to identify suspected cases among contacts of infected poultry. 
Adequate quantity of Tamilflu and personal protective equipments are available to meet 
any exigency. 
There is active surveillance for those who had come in to contact with poultry and all 
those reported to have symptoms of even upper respiratory tract infections are isolated and 
kept under observation following strict infection control practices. There are however no 
reports of any human cases of Avian Influenza. 
Earlier, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare had intimated a number of preparedness 
measures which includes monitoring by inter ministerial group, nation consultation and 
preparation of contingency plan which has been circulated to all State and districts, 
stockpiling of oseltamivir (Tamilflu) and personal protective equipments etc. 
The situation is being closely monitored and under control.

Health care for all in Uttaranchal 
662. SHRIHARISH RAWAT: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any target for taking health care to all parts of Uttaranchal has been 
fixed; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government are aware that CD's Health Committee and some other 
important Heart Institutes has recommended some measures in this behalf; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the action Government have proposed to take in the 
matter? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) The Government has 
lanuched the National Rural Health Mission in April, 2005 for providing effective 
healthcare to the rural population through out the country with special focus on 18 States 
with poor health indicators and weak health infrastructure. The Mission adopts a synergistic 
approach by relating health to determinants of good health and the main objective is to 
provide accessible, affordable and accountable healthcare especially to the poor and 
vulnerable sections. It is an articulation of the commitment of the Government to raise public 
spending on Health from 0.9% of GDP to 2-3% of GDP over the next five years. Under 
the strategy of NRHM, the gaps in the existing scenario of rural health care is to be 
addressed through involvement of the community, the panchayati raj institutions and other 
non-governmental ogranizations. An accredited social health activist will act as a link 
between the community and the health care system. The State of Uttaranchal has been 
included in the list of high focused 18 States. 
(c) and (d) The Cll National Committee on Health Care commissioned Mckinsey and 
Company for a study to define the way forward for healthcare. This study has also 
reiterated the need for higher levels of investment as already contained in the National 
Health Policy 2002 and the National Common Minimum Programme to meet the 
increased demands of the Health Sector. In fact recognizing the gap in the provision of 
health care services against the existing demand, efforts have been made to enhance the 
allocations under Health particularly with the launch of the National Rural Health 
Mission.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) No,

to the notice of Government of India. The Government of India do not maintain 
details of such incidents. Information supplied by various States during the 
last two years regarding such incidents are enclosed as statement. (See below) 
(c) to (e) A Review Committee was constituted as per the Delhi High Court 
Judgement dated 6.9.2004 in W.P. No. 813/2004 to review the provision of 
the Transplantation of Human Organ Act, 1994 and the Transplantation of 
Human Organ Rules, 1995. The final report of the Committee has been 
received by the Government. The synopsis of the recommendations made by 
Review Committee are broadly as under:— 
(i) It may be mandatory that all cases of near relative donor also be routed 
through authorization committee. 
(ii) Guidelines for working of authorization committee have been laid 
down. 
(iii) Testing to establish genetic relationship and histocompability should 
be done in the laboratories ap proved by Directorate of Health 
Services. 
(iv) ORBO activities should be expanded. 
(v) A national organ transplant pr ogramme with special emphasis on 
cadaver donations be promoted. 
(vi) Every hospital should make it mandatory for ICU/treating medical staff 
to make requests to relative of brain dead patient for organ donation 
and should report all brain dead potential donor to ORBO. 
(vii) There should be incentives for the family for Cadaver Organ Donor. 
(viii) Simplification of Rules for procedure have been suggested. 
The Government is examining the Re port of the Review Committee for 
implementation in phases.

Statement 
The salient features of the National Steel Policy 
• The NSP sets out a broad roadmap for the Indian Steel Industry in its 
journey towards reform, restructuring and globalization. 
• The long-term goal of the NSP is that India should have a modern and 
efficient steel industry of world standards, catering to diversified steel 
demand. The focus of the policy is to achieve global competitiveness 
not only in term of cost, quality and product-mix but also in terms of 
global benchmarks of efficiency and productivity. 
248 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
• In order to achieve the goal of 110 million tonnes of steel production by 
2019-20, the NSP seeks to remove the supply-side constraints to the 
growth of this industry in an open, globally integrated and competitive 
environment. 
• The NSP seeks to adopt a multi-pronged strategy to move towards the 
long-term policy goal. On the demand side, the strategy would be to 
create incremental demand through promotional efforts, creation of 
awareness and strengthening the delivery chain, particularly in rural 
areas. On the supply side, the strategy would be to facilitate creation of 
additional capacity, remove procedural and policy bottlenecks in the 
availability of inputs such as iron ore and coal, make higher 
investments in R&D and encourage the creation of infrastructure such 
as roads, railways, and ports. 
• The NSP acknowledges the low per capita consumption of steel in the 
country, especially in the rural areas and the need to boost steel 
consumption to improve quality of life and help in meeting the 
growing aspirations of masses. 
• In order to achieve the strategic goal of 110 mt of steel production by 
2019-20, the industry would need additional capital. In addition, 
funds would be required for technological upgrade of existing 
facilities. In order to mobilize such vast resources NSP seeks to 
encourage foreign direct investment In addition the policy also seeks 
to make the fiscal incentives, ava ilable to infrastructure projects, 
accessible to the steel industry. 
• The NSP seeks to support developing of risk-hedging instruments like 
futures and derivatives to contain price volatility in the steel market. 
• The NSP seeks to strengthen the existing training and research 
facilities available to the domestic steel industry so as to provide 
suitable training programmes especially for the secondary small-scale 
units and also to collect and analyze data on important parameters of 
the industry. 
• The NSP seeks to mount aggre ssive R&D efforts to create 
manufacturing capability for special types of steel, substitute coking 
249 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2006] 
coal, use iron ore fines, develop new products suited to rural needs, 
enhance material and energy efficiency, utilize waste, and arrest 
environmental degradation. 
• The NSP acknowledges the important role played by the secondary 
steel sector in providing empl oyment, meeting local demand of 
steel in rural and semi-urban area, and meeting the country's 
demand of some special products and seeks to endeavour to 
provide the necessary feedstock to these units at reasonable prices 
from major plants through the existing mechanism of State Small 
Industries Corporations. 
• The NSP recognizes the fact that  integration of the Indian steel 
industry with the global economy requires that the industry should 
be protected from unfair trade practices, which become common 
especially during periods of downturn. The NSP therefore, 
envisages institution of mechanisms for import surveillance, and 
monitoring export subsidies in other countries.

GOVERNMENT BILL 
The Government of Union Territories and The Government of 
National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Bill, 2006 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ. V PATIL): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, I beg to move. 
"  That the Bill further to amend the government of Union Territories 
Act, 1963 and the Government of National Capital Territory of 
Delhi Act, 1991, betaken into consideration." 
Sir, the second proviso to article 82 and the second proviso to 
article 170(3) of the Constitution provide that readjustment of 
constituencies after the delimitation exercise will take only from such 
date as the President may, by order, specify, and until such readjustment 
takes effect, any election to the House shall be held on the basis of 
territorial constituencies existing before such readjustment. In other words, 
the Delimitation Orders, issued by  the Delimitation Commission under 
the Delimitation Act, 2002, in which the constituencies will be readjusted 
on the basis of 2001, Census, will take effect only from such date as the 
President may, by order, specify, and till such time, elections will be held 
on the basis of 1971 Census. 
As far as Union Territory of Pondicherry and the National Capital 
Territory of Delhi are concerned, there is no such provision empowering 
the President of the Central Government to specify the date from which 
280 

[24 February, 2006] RAJ YA SABHA 
1.00 P.M. 
The delimitation will take effect. There is, therefore, an inconsistency 
between the provisions applicable to the State and the Union Territories. 
The delimitation exercise in respect of Union Territory of Pondicherry 
has been completed but in the case of  the majority of States and the 
National Capital Territory of Delhi, the exercise is in progress. Hence, an 
anomalous situation will arise in which elections may have to be conducted 
on the basis of delimitation based on 2001 Census in the Union Territory 
of Pondicherry, but in the rest of the country, the elections would be held 
on the basis of the 1971 Census. 
The Bill seeks to rectify the aforesaid anomalous situation arising out 
of lack of a suitable enabling provison in the Government of Union 
Territories Act, 1963 and the Government of the National Capital Territory 
of Delhi Act, 1963 and the Government of the National Capital Territory 
of Delhi Act, 1991, by inserting a provision similar to the corresponding 
provisions under the second proviso to article 82 and the second proviso 
to clause (3) of article 170 of the Constitution in the Government of Union 
Territories Act, 1963 with retrospective effect, that is from 31st March, 
2005, and the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991, 
from the date of assent of the Bill. With these words I commend the Bill 
to this august House for approval.

SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Chairman, Sir, 
the population census in the country shows that the number of girls has 
been falling steadily for the past two decades as compared to the number 
of boys. For every 1,000 boys up to the age of six, the number of girls 
dropped from" 962 in 1981 to 945 in 1991 and 927 in 2001. It is a fact that 
the ratio of number of females per thousand male is falling in many States 
in the country even today. Despite a legal ban in india on sex selection of 
babies, this practice is still widely prevalent and it is estimated that, at 
284 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
least, 10 million female births may have been aborted in the past 20 
years.

medical establishments by an independent committee to find out indirect 
evidences of violation of PNDT Act. It is, nevertheless, recognized that mere 
legislation if not enough to deal with this problem that has roots in social 
behaviours and prejudices. The Government should undertake various 
activities to create mass awarenes s against the practices of prenatal 
determination of sex and female foeticide through radio, television and print 
media units. The Government should also organize workshops and seminars 
through voluntary organizations at the block, district, regional and State levels to 
create awareness against this social evil. Participation of religious leaders as 
well as medical fraternity will definitely improve the situation much better to 
curb this practice.

order to protect the girl child in our country.

Need to take immediate measures to control Chickungunya Virus 
in Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Chairman, Sir, on 
the One hand the Government is moving heaven and earth to control Bird 
Flu, but on the other, the State of Andhra Pradesh is reeling under 
mysterious virus which has spread its tentacles in six districts of Andhra 
Pradesh, including the capital. The State has faced dengue and encephalitis 
just a few months back and now it is the turn of Chickungunya. The blood 
samples of Chickungunya from State tested at the National Institute of 
virology confirmed that the virus is Chickungunya. More than 1400 cases 
in just a few days have been reported in various villages of the above 
districts. This virus was first discovered in Kenya in 1952. Then, in 1965, 
it had affected three lakh people in Chennai. And, now, after four decades, it 
resurfaced again in Andhra Pradesh. The medical experts from the NIV 
say that this has come from Kyasanur forest in Karnatakav The symptoms 
of Chickungunya are high fever, excruciating pain in the joints and 
headache. The State Government is not able to control it because the 
symptoms are confused with dengue and the villagers are caught unaware 
to find out as to what kind of disease it is. The State Government has set 
up medical camps to treat the patients. But, since the number of cases is 
going up, it is proved to be a difficult task for the State Government. 
Hence, I request the Government of India to immediately send the Central 
medical teams and medicines to Andhra Pradesh to assist the State in 
controlling this deadly virus.

Concern over decline in Wheat Production in the Country 
SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE (Assam): India's wheat 
292 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
production climbed steadily during past three decades at 76 million tonnes but 
production has dropped by 1.1 million tonnes per-year and average yield since 
2000 has been 70 million tonnes. If the trend continues, India may not be able to 
meet projected demand of 109 million tonnes for the year 2020. We should not be 
complacent. According to scientists in States of Northern Gangetic plains 
improper use of fertilizers had led to widespread deficiency of micronutrients 
such as zinc, magnesium and sulphur elements that are crucial for successful 
plant growth. Farmers in Punjab, Haryana and U.P. have tended to use excess of 
urea, ignoring need for other micronutrients and the continued use of urea, year 
after year, has depleted micronutrients on farmland. If micronutrients level drops 
critical level, urea will not be able to boost crop yield. Besides, climatic change 
also is the reason for drop in production. Wheat yields have also remained stuck 
because new high-yielding varieties are not available to the farmers. Also other 
economic factors have pushed farmers away from wheat as input costs of 
water-pumping, fertilizers and pesticides have gone up whereas minimum 
support price remained static. I will request the Government to have a 
thorough study conducted into the problems of scarcity of wheat production by 
an Expert Committee which should also suggest measures for boosting up 
wheat production so that India's food security may not be at stake.

Need to Set Up a Regulatory Body to Oversee Road Safety on 
National Highways 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY (Andhra Predesh): Sir, a 
well- Knit and coordinated system of transport plays an important role in 
the sustained economic growth of any country. India has one of the largest 
road networks in the world, aggregating to about 3.32 million kilometres. 
Of this, National and State Highways account for 1,95,000 kilometres. Of 
this, National Highways and Expressways constitute 65,000 kilometres— 
1.94 per cent of the total length of road—and they carry 45 per cent of 
the total traffic of India. 
The strain on this network is increasing day-by-day. This becomes 
clear if one looks at the growing number of vehicles. Vehicles have been 
growing at 10.16 per cent per annum over the last five years. The 
percentage of freight traffic has also increased to 61 per cent. In order to 
give boost to the economic development, Government of India embarked 
upon the NHDP to upgrade the National Highways to 4, 6 or 8 lanes. 
Sir, new National Highways and Expressways allow traffic to move at 
high speeds and thereby increase the risk of accidents. Many sources, 
including Planning Commission, recognized this as a source of-big 
concern. This becomes clear if one looks at the increasing number of 
road accidents on the newly constructed highways and expressways. 
According to the UN, 90,000 people are being killed every year in India. 
The economic cost of such accidents is Rs. 50,000 crores. 
Therefore, there is an urgent need for setting up uniform safety 
standards and a regulatory body to oversee the safety standards and 
also to look into the acceptable gradients based on international standards. 
Even the Committee on Infrastructure has recommended such a body.

seen a city girl marrying a farmer's sons? A city girl might marry the son 
of a Director of a sugar factory or the son of a Minister who happens to 
have land. But city girls have stopped marrying children of farmers 
because they know that if she is ma rried into a farmer's family her life 
will be entirely miserable and, therefore, she turns her back. We have 
all this experience but we never register it. In 1980, for the first time, Sir, 
! made a calculation that the loss that is caused to farmers because of 
the adverse governmental price policies was of the order of Rs. 10,000 
crores. Later on, Ashok Gulati, who has now become internationally 
famous for his work on negative subsidies wrote his thesis and said 
that the loss caused to the farm ers because of the anti-farmers 
governmental policies was of the orde r of Rs. 10,000 crore. It is the 
same figure. The official economist lobby, at the same time, was saying 
that farmers are heavily subsidised. In fact, Ashok Mitra, the famous 
Communist-Economist, in his book 'Terms of Trade and Class Relations' 
actually states that I ndian farmers are so heavily subsidised that they 
are the better-off people in this country and that is why they have got the 
335 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2006] 
reins of political power. Can you imagine a more absurd statement from 
a person who claims to be an economist? But the Communists have 
always been wrong about their agricultural doctrines, whether it is Marx, 
Lenin or Stalin. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIAN): Nobody is here, then 
why are you saying this? 
SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI: They will, probably, read about 
it. Then, the question is: how can this happen? For example, till 1965, 
that is, the epoch of Pandit Nehru, as Mr. Narayansamy has mentioned, 
if the farmer had good crops, the prices fell and nobody came to support 
them. And, if we had bad crops and there was a famine, then the farmers 
would be forced to give levy of foodgrains and the levy prices were often 
much less than the market prices. Very often, it happened that the farmers 
had to purchase the jawar in Maharashtra at elevated prices and give 
them at lower prices as levy. That was the kind of exploitation that was 
taking place. In case of sugar, when I got into the farmers' agitation, 70 
per cent of the sugar was taken away as levy at a price which was just 
50 per cent of the market price. There was a period when my friend, 
who used to be a Member of this House, Shri Bhupendra Singh Mann, 
was punished by the Court because he was carrying just five kilos of 
wheat from Punjab to Haryana and crossing the State borders with wheat 
commodities was a punishable offence. In Maharashtra, till recently, 
cotton could not be given to Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh even 
though the prices there were Rs. 200 to Rs. 300 per quintal higher than 
the prices offered by cotton monopoly. When the farmers could get better 
prices for onion, there would be  an immediate ban on the export of 
onion with the result that the price of onion came down. This was a 
systematic manner in which the Government of India right till 1965 and 
even much later, deliberately depressed agricultural prices. I am using 
the word 'deliberately', and I am going to support it. You will find that 
deliberation in Shri V.T. Krishnamachari's introduction to the Second 
Five Year Plan, where he said in effect that if you want to have socialist 
industries, then you would have to take away the surplus from agriculture 
in order to develop primary capital for the socialist industry. Now, this 
was exactly what was said in the Soviet Union in the days of Stalin, by 
Praebrozensky and Bukharin. Stalin sent tanks on Russian farmers 
calling them kulaks. We did not use any uncouth methods like that. We 
336 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
used rather sophisticated and civil methods but the effect was equally 
disastrous. In brief, what happened was that after 1947, the British went 
away, but the British policies continued. I can say that if the white British 
left, their place was taken by brown British and the policies continued to 
be the same. The beneficiaries were no more Lancashire and 
Machester, they were probably Kolkata and Mumbai, but the policies 
remained the same. Since 1980, we have had a running debate with the 
official economists who claim that the farmers have very high subsidies, 
and those like me who claimed that the farmers have negative subsidy. 
And, I had to explain to them what the negative subsidy is, and the 
way I explained it was very simple. I think, I should say it even here. Sir, 
after I became a farmer, one of the first crops I took was cucumber 
because in Pune, cucumber was a famous variety. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIAN): Please, wind up. 
SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI: When I started sending them 
to Bombay — at that time it was Bombay and not Mumbai — I got 
communication saying that they had sold my cucumber and I would get 
about Rs. 300. The second time, I got Rs. 128. The third time, I got a 
letter saying that they had sold it to the best of their capacity of cucumbers 
but the proceeds could not cover even the transport and the portage 
and, therefore, I should send them Rs. 138. so, they sold my cucumber; 
they kept the money and wanted me to give them additional Rs. 138. 
Now, this is what I call negative subsidy - when the price realised by the 
farmer is less than the cost of production of the farmer or when the price 
that the farmer receives is le~ss than the price that he would have realised 
in a hypothetical^ free market, then it is called negative sussidy. What I 
said was finally vindicated in 1986 to 1989 when on the occasion of the 
WTO negotiations, Mr. Pranab Mukherjee, the then Commerce Minister, 
made a statement. He made a statement that it is a fact that in India a 
negative subsidy was imposed on farmers. This is a confession. This is 
not a party matter. And, at the same time, Japan made a declaration to 
the WTO that our price policies are such that if the cost of production is 
100 rupees then the farmers should get 190 rupees. The European Union 
made a statement that our policies are such that if the cost of production 
is 100 rupees, then the farmers should get 165 rupees, and, the United 
States stated that our policies are such that if the cost of production is $ 
100, the farmer should get $ 135. The Government of India under the 
337 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2006] 
signature of Shri Pranab Mukherjee — I had discussed this matter with him 
even at that time — gave a categorical statement that our policies are such 
that even if the cost of production is 183 rupees, the farmer will not get more 
than 100 rupee! There were some disputes, statistical dispute and 
theoretical dispute as to whether that was 118 or 183 but there was no 
dispute about the fact that the farmers have always worked under the 
negative subsidy. 
Even on the eve of leaving for Hong Kong, the present Minister for 
Commerce, Shri Kamal Nath admitted that even today, the Indian farmers are 
working under a system of negative subsidy. If it is this negative subsidy that 
makes agriculture a losing proposition, then, naturally the solution in Part 4 of 
the resolution have to 'change'. For example, examining the remedies 
proposed by Narayanasamy, we come to. He talks of the waiver of loans, he 
talks of fresh loans being made available, he talks of procurement policies 
being improved, and, he also talks of a system of insurance and of a better 
system of market intervention. All these things give an impression as if the 
farmers can survive only if there is a godfather in the Government. This kind 
of an approach, in case of a farmer  who actually carries out a physical 
multiplication of income shows that there is something which is hidden. 
What I would say is — Dr. Gill also raised that point — that it is a fact that in 
the present epoch, we would have difficulty in competing with countries like 
America and Europe because they have larger farms, they are highly 
subsidised and mechanised, they have technology. A Kisan leader in Uttar 
Pradesh said, United States and Europe are like wrestlers who have been fed 
on badam and other nutritious things while our farmers have been starved for 
fifty years. How do you expect our starved farmers to have competition with the 
world-class wrestlers? I would like to say that that wrestler has some weak 
points. Dr. Gill also mentioned that we have a great endowment of solar 
energy, abundant sun shine, and, we have adequate water resources; and 
that is going to clinch, that is going to be a factor to finally decide as to who will win 
in the international competition. What is required is that we ought to make up. It 
is not that we are asking for favours from the Government. As the 
Chairman of the Task Force on agriculture to advise the previous Prime 
Ministers on the WTO situation, Sir, I know, and, it is a factually established 
statistical data, that in the year 1996-97 according to the Government's 
statistics 
338 

[24 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
— in one year alone, the loss caused to the farmers because of the 
negative policies of the Government was Rs. 1,13,000 crores. All this is in 
Government's document and, we calculated that since 1980 till 2001, the loss 
caused to the farmers because of the anti-farmer governmental policies was 
as mush as 300 thousand crores of rupees. That is the sum that the 
Government owes the farmers. 
Don't talk of how much money the farmers owe to the banks, how much 
money they have to pay for the electricity. The important thing is that the 
Govt, has taken away 300 thousand crores of rupees from them. That is, 
probably, as Lord Keynes said, "In Economics bygones are bygones". We 
cannot go back on but, what is important is that when the Government spend 
at least Rs. 300,000 on providing the infrastructure, that would make the 
farmer competitive in the global market. For example, we need to 
have'some of the important things. The first thing, I would like to say—I hope 
Mr. Narayanasamy is listening — is that the agriculture shuold be privatised. 
Today, agriculture is highly dominated by the State. The land belongs to the 
Government, you know the principle of eminence juris, therefore, the farmer is 
only a sort of a holder or a tenant of the land and the land can be taken away 
from the farmer at the pleasure of the Government. This is a thing which 
discourages farmers from carrying out any investment in the land. 
Secondly, the inputs are all controlled by the Government and, 
therefore, the prices often are higher than the prices in the competing 
countries. What we will have to do is to open up so that the Indian farmers get 
their inputs at about the same price as the farmers elsewhere. Thirdly, Sir, there 
should be an opening up of the output markets as well. India is not one 
market. India is a fractured market and before we go into a globalised 
system, where the division of labour is carried out according to the comparative 
advantage, we ought to have a specialisation between various regions in India, 
depending upon the comparative advantage. For example, there is absolutely 
no reason why Bengal should specialise in jute. There are other States which 
can produce much better jute at a much lower cost. But that kind of a 
division of labour, that kind of an apportionment and allocation of resources 
can take place only in a market economy; in a Government-controlled 
economy, that kind of a rationalisation is impossible. Then, we need to have 
is we should have a sophisticated market, and I congratulate the present 
Government- 
339 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2006] 
Narayanasamy/7, if you are listening - I am glad that the system of 
Agriculture Produce Marketing Committees is being withdrawn and we 
are encouraging the system of or ganised retail trade. And, .1 must 
congratulate the present Finance Minister because he has allowed even 
the Foregin Direct Investment in retail trade. Further, need to have an 
informatics infrastructure and a network as well where the farmers who 
have to go into the global market will be able to see on the internet what 
kind of prices are prevailing in different markets, what are the arrivals 
and what are the departures in different countries. 
Then, Sir, we ought to have a large network of scientific laboratories. 
If you want to go into global market, you must know what is the quality of 
your products. How can you know that, unless you have a laboratory 
nearby? 
Unfortunately, when the Food Safety and Standards Bill was being 
discussed, we found that in the country, as a whole, there were only 17 
laboratories which could take care of the whole range of product. What 
we need to have is, every science college at a tehsil place upgraded into 
a scientific laboratory that can become a food-testing laboratory. That is 
what will do good to the farmers. 
Sir, the last solution which I would offer to Mr. Narayanasamy is an 
important solution and that is the point that Mr. Pilania mentioned. The 
land is treated as mother therefore, sacred, etc. It is just a lot of 
nonsensical poetry My experience sh ows that every farmer and every 
farmer's son, who gets a chance to find a job to get into the industry or 
a trade, leave agriculture because he knows where his survival is. 
Therefore, we ought to provide a land market, a developed land market, 
and, I am glad that the Deputy Chai rmen of the Planning Commission, 
Dr. Montek Singh Ahluwalia, has accepted this suggestion. We ought to 
permit the farmers, who find themse lves psychologically or physically 
incapable of meeting the challenges of the global market, to leave. And, 
if there are others, who have better managerial abilities and who have 
more investible funds, should come in. We have been following a policy 
where even Amitabh Bachchan cannot become a farmer unless he 
produces a certain certificate. Sir, I had difficulty in becoming a farmer 
after returning from the United Nations. I was allowed to become a farmer 
only when in one year my annual income came to less than Rs. 10,000. 
340 

[24 February, 2006] RAJ YA SABHA 
If you are poor enough, you can become a farmer. But if you have money, 
then you cannot become a farmer. That  is the kind of wrong exit and 
entry policy for the agriculture which will have to be removed. 
The Green Revolution succeeded. And the Green Revolution meant 
employment of the hybrid seeds, employment of chemical fertilizers and 
chemical pesticides, and new technology. Now, this was not within the 
intellectual or mental scope of many people, but they were able to leave 
the agriculture at that time because of a large number of anh-jamindari 
Acts and Land Ceiling Acts. That is how Late P.V. Narasimha Rao's 
forefathers were able to leave their 3000 acres of land in Andhra Pradesh 
and come out and later on prosper in Delhi. The reluctant farmer will 
have given some kind of a golden handshake and some kind of a 
voluntary retirement scheme for t he farmers who find life impossible. 
Today, farmers are committing suicides because there is no exit, they 
are sort of trapped, and they will have to be provided some vent if you 
want to bring down the number of suicides. Before concluding, I once 
again congratulate Shri V. Narayansamy for having provided a very broad 
canvass permitting a comprehensive discussion of various issues and 
more importantly not just description of how miserable the farmer is but 
also discussion of why. has it happened despite the British exit, despite 
the moneylender going away, and despite the jamindars going away, the 
farmer continues to be in a situation much worse than he ever was 
under the British regime. Thank you very much, Sir.

SHRIV. NARAYANASAMY: Hon. Vice-Chairman, Sir, thank you very much for 
giving me this opportunity. The hon. Minister has intervened. I am grateful to him. I am 
grateful to the hon. Members who have participated in the discussion. Thirteen hon. 
Members participated in the discussion. They are Shri E.M. Sudarsana Naatchiappan, 
Shri Suresh Bhardwaj, Shri A. Vijayaraghavan, Shri Ravula Chandra Sekarfteddy, 
Shrimati Kum Kum Rai, Shri Harendra Singh Malik, Dr. Faguni Ram, Shri Jayantilal 
Barot, Dr. M.S. Gill, Or. Gyan Prakash Pilania, Shri Sharad Anantrao Joshi, Dr. 
(Shrimati) Prabha Thakur and Shri Moolchand Meena. I am very grateful to all the 
hon. Members. The entire House has shown its concern for the farmers. Every part of 
my Resolution was discussed by the hon. Members. They gave their viewpoints about 
how to mitigate the sufferings of farmers. It is a universal phenomenon that the farmer 
is at the receiving end. We all speak about them. I am not going into any party-political 
consideration. Every political party tells the people that they are for the Kisans. Every 
governments tells them that they are for the welfare of the farmers. In the country, 70 per 
cent people belong to the farming community. They are the creators of economy of this 
country. But the benefit is taken away by industrialists and the business community. 
Whatever is produced by farmers, that goes to the industry and the market. The 
intermediaries, the businessmen earn income out of it and the farmer is at a loss. 
Whether at the production 
347 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2006] 
stage or when the produce goes to the market, the farmers are the 
worst sufferers. Moreover, earlier the farmers were given subsidy for 
fertilizers, seeds, etc. They were given subsidy for implements also. 
Gradually, in the name of modernisation and in the name of a changed-
economy, some of the benefits have been withdrawn. In the world 
economic forum, that is WTO, we have been fighting so that our farmers 
can get their due. The reason is, the Western countries, the developed 
countries, are giving more than 70 per cent subsidy to the farmers 
because they want the produce to go up. They know that if they don't do 
it the farmers will stop cultivation in those countries. The United States 
is giving more than 60 per cent subsidy to their farmers. The European 
countries are also giving subsidy to the farmers. Now the suggestion 
which I have made is this. We have discussed in this august House one 
issue of reducing rate of interest  on bank loans, whether it is the 
cooperative institution or a bank. The hon. Finance Minister was trying 
to defend himself, but in vain. The hon. Finance Minister said that the 
money was going to the cooperative banks at an interest rate of 5.5 per 
cent and then they add their cost overheads and that it comes to 16 to 
17 peP cent; but up to Rs. 50,000,' we are giving loan at an interest rate 
of 9 per cent. That is what the Finance Minister said. The cost of input 
for farmers is very high. They are ail small farmers because they are 
having small holdings up to two acres of land. In our country rich farmers 
are not more than 5 to 6 per cent. Up to Rs. 3 lakhs, the rate of interest 
should be very low. If we compare it with the Western countries, in the 
Western countries the rate of interest is 1 to 2 per cent, even for 
agriculture. An hon. Member rightly put a question to the Finance Minister 
that when you are giving loan for purchasing a vehicle, for purchasing a 
house, for purchasing a refrigerator and  other things at zero per cent 
interest rate, why should it not be for agriculture also? The farmer is 
overburdened because of the compou nding interest. Therefore, they 
are committing suicides. We want that the farmers should be relieved of 
their indebtedness. I have got with me  a sample survey conducted by 
an organisation. In Andhra Pradesh alone, 82 per cent of the farmers 
are in debt. In Tamil Nadu, 74.5 per cent farmers are in debt. They are 
indebted to whom. They are indebted to private moneylenders, apart 
from banks. So far as Punjab is concerned, the number is 65.4 per cent; 
in the case of Kerala, it is 64.4 per cent; in the case of Karnataka, it is 
348 

[24 February, 2006] RAJ YA SABHA 
61.6 per cent and in the case of Maharashtra, it is 54.8 per cent. The 
basic reason for committing suicide is, the farmers are indebted to private 
moneylenders. The private moneyl enders are squeezing them. The 
farmers are unable to repay the money. Therefore, they are going to the 
extent of ending their life. So, until and unless the Government supports 
the farmers in raising their crops, suicides cannot stop. Otherwise, the 
private moneylenders go to the farmers and give them money. The 
innocent farmers take money from then, and they get into the debt trap. 
As the Finance Minister mentione d, the co-operative system—trje 
system itself is in shambles—has to be revamped. The hon. Prime 
Minister has allocated Rs. 35 crores for revamping the co-operative 
system in the country. In various places, I have seen that the co-operative 
banks and co-operative institutions have become somebody's private 
property. 
Federalism is not there; the democratic system is not here in the co-
operative system. Unless and until the Cooperatives Act is amended 
and a stringent law is brought, it will become somebody's own property 
and our poor farmers cannot enjoy the fruit of it. And, the theory of co-
operative system itself will change. 
Sir, since the hon. Minister has said  that he would take note of the 
suggestions by various hon. Members, I would only mention in brief the 
suggestions that I wish to place before him. No.1 is compensatory 
insurance; No.2 is increasing the subsidy; No.3 is farmers' credit policy 
and No.4 is technology upgradation. Now, when we talk about lab to 
land, in our country, we have seen that even though a lot of inventions 
have been made, it takes eight to ten years—the hon. S & T Minister is 
here—for any invention to reach the farmers. By then the whole system 
changes and the benefit does not accrue to them. Therefore, the lab to 
land has to be immediately adopted. Also, there should be cold storage 
facility made available to farmers.  Good market inte rvention by the 
Government is also very important. Otherwise, it will only benefit the 
middlemen and the businesmen. Therefore, unless and until market 
intervention by the Government is ther e, it will be very difficult for any 
farmer to survive. Sir, i am sure that the hon. Minister has taken note of 
our suggestions, and he would, in due consultation with the Finance 
Minister, evolve the credit policy for the farmers. That is very important.

beginning. As of now, let the farmers be relieved of their debt. 
Sir, with these words, since the hon. Minister has requested me to 
withdraw my Resolution, I hope he wi ll accept my suggestions and

them.
